18.0: As usual, Lily thought. At that exact moment there was always something that had to be done — something Mrs. Ramsay, for private reasons, had decided to do at once, even if, as now, everyone was standing around making jokes, unable to make up their minds whether to go to the smoking-room, the drawing-room or up to the attics. And then, in the middle of all the noise, you would see Mrs. Ramsay standing there with Minta’s arm in hers, suddenly recollect, “Yes, it’s time for that now,” and slip off at once, secretive, to do something by herself. The minute she left, things began to fall apart. People drifted, hesitated, went their separate ways. Mr. Bankes took Charles Tansley by the arm and headed for the terrace to finish the political argument they had started over dinner, and that shifted the whole balance of the evening, tipped its weight another way. Watching them go, and catching a word or two about Labour Party policy, Lily felt as though the two men had climbed up to the ship’s bridge to take their bearings; that was how the switch from poetry to politics struck her. So off they went, Mr. Bankes and Charles Tansley, while the rest stood and watched Mrs. Ramsay climbing the stairs alone in the lamplight. Where, Lily wondered, was she off to in such a hurry?
18.1: In fact she was not running or hurrying at all; if anything she went rather slowly. After all that talk, she felt like standing still for a moment and picking out one particular thing — the thing that mattered — detaching it, setting it apart, cleaning off all the emotions and odds and ends that clung to it, so that she could hold it up in front of her and bring it before the court where the judges she had appointed to decide such matters sat assembled in council. Is it good, is it bad, is it right or wrong? Where are we all heading? and so on. In this way she recovered her balance after the shock of what had happened, and without knowing it, and rather absurdly, she used the elm branches outside to help steady herself. Her world was changing; the trees were still. The event had given her a feeling of motion. Everything had to be put in order. That must be set right, and that, she thought, silently admiring how dignified the trees were in their stillness, and then again the magnificent upward sweep of the elm branches (like a ship’s prow riding up a wave) when the wind lifted them. For there was a wind (she paused to look out). There was a wind, so that every so often the leaves brushed aside to uncover a star, and the stars themselves seemed to tremble and dart light, straining to flash out between the leaves’ edges. Yes, then, that was done, finished; and like everything finished, it had turned solemn. Thought of now, stripped of chatter and emotion, it seemed to have been there forever and only now revealed; and in being revealed it fixed everything firmly in place. No matter how long they lived, she thought, walking on, they would return to this night, this moon, this wind, this house — and to her as well. It flattered her, in the place where she was most open to flattery, to think that however long they lived she would be woven into their hearts, wound among them; and this, and this, and this, she thought as she climbed, laughing — but lovingly — at the sofa on the landing (her mother’s), at the rocking-chair (her father’s), at the map of the Hebrides. All of it would be brought back to life in Paul’s and Minta’s lives. “The Rayleys” — she tried out the new name. And with her hand on the nursery door she felt that sense of shared feeling with others that emotion brings, as though the dividing walls had worn so thin that practically (it was a feeling of relief and happiness) everything flowed in one stream; the chairs, the tables, the maps were hers, were theirs, whose did not matter; and Paul and Minta would carry it on after she was dead.
18.2: Firmly, so it wouldn’t squeak, she turned the handle and went in, her lips pressed together a little as though reminding herself not to talk out loud. But the instant she was inside she saw, irritated, that there had been no need for care. The children were awake. It was really too annoying. Mildred ought to be more careful. James was wide awake, Cam was sitting bolt upright, Mildred was out of bed in her bare feet, it was nearly eleven, and every one of them was talking. What was wrong? That horrid skull again. She had asked Mildred to move it, but of course Mildred had forgotten, and now here were Cam and James, both wide awake and squabbling, when they should have been asleep hours ago. Whatever had made Edward send them this horrid skull? It had been silly of her to let them nail it up there. It was nailed on tight, Mildred said, and Cam couldn’t get to sleep with it in the room, and James screamed if anybody touched it.
18.3: Then Cam must go to sleep (it had great big horns, Cam said) — must go to sleep and dream about lovely palaces, said Mrs. Ramsay, sitting down beside her on the bed. Cam said she could see the horns all over the room. And so she could. Wherever they set the light (and James couldn’t sleep without one), a shadow fell somewhere.
18.4: “But think, Cam, it’s just an old pig,” Mrs. Ramsay said, “a nice black pig, like the ones at the farm.” Cam, though, thought it was a horrid thing, sending its branches at her from every corner of the room.
18.5: “All right, then,” said Mrs. Ramsay, “we’ll cover it up.” They all watched as she went to the chest of drawers and pulled open the little drawers one after another, fast; and when nothing in them would do, she whipped off her own shawl and wrapped it around the skull, round and round and round. Then she went back to Cam, laid her head almost flat on the pillow next to Cam’s, and told her how lovely it looked now; how the fairies would love it; it was like a bird’s nest; it was like a beautiful mountain of the kind she had seen abroad, with valleys and flowers and bells ringing and birds singing and little goats and antelopes. … As she said the words, rhythmically, she could see them echoing in Cam’s mind; Cam was saying after her that it was like a mountain, a bird’s nest, a garden, and there were little antelopes, and her eyes kept opening and closing. And Mrs. Ramsay kept on, ever more monotonous, ever more rhythmic and nonsensical, telling her to shut her eyes and sleep and dream of mountains and valleys and stars falling and parrots and antelopes and gardens and everything lovely, she said — lifting her head very slowly and speaking more and more mechanically — until she was sitting upright and could see that Cam had fallen asleep.
18.6: Now, she whispered, going across to his bed, James had to go to sleep too, because look, she said, the boar’s skull was still there; nobody had touched it; they’d done exactly what he wanted; there it was, not hurt at all. He checked that the skull really was still under the shawl. But there was something else he wanted to ask her. Would they be going to the Lighthouse tomorrow?
18.7: No, she said, not tomorrow, but soon, she promised — the next fine day. He was very good about it. He lay down, and she pulled the covers over him. But he would never forget, she knew; and she felt angry with Charles Tansley, with her husband and with herself, because she was the one who had raised his hopes. Then, reaching for her shawl and remembering that it was wrapped around the boar’s skull, she stood up and lowered the window another inch or two. She heard the wind and breathed in the chill night air, which did not care at all; she murmured good night to Mildred, left the room, let the latch-tongue slide slowly out into the lock, and was gone.
18.8: She hoped he wouldn’t go banging his books on the floor above their heads, she thought, still dwelling on how irritating Charles Tansley was. Neither child was a good sleeper; they were excitable, and a man who could say such things about the Lighthouse seemed to her quite likely to knock over a pile of books just as they were dropping off, clumsily sweeping them off the table with his elbow. She assumed, that is, that he had gone up to work. And yet he looked so forlorn; and yet it would be a relief when he left; and yet she would see to it that he was treated better tomorrow; and yet he was wonderful with her husband; and yet his manners really did need improving; and yet she liked the way he laughed — and as she thought this, coming down the stairs, she noticed that the moon itself was now visible through the staircase window, the yellow harvest moon, and she turned; and they looked up and saw her standing above them on the stairs.
18.9: “That’s my mother,” Prue thought. Yes; Minta ought to look at her; Paul Rayley ought to look at her. There is the thing itself, she felt, as if there were only one such person in the whole world — her mother. A moment ago, chatting with the others, she had been completely grown-up; now she turned into a child again, and what they had been up to was a game, and she wondered whether her mother would allow their game or forbid it. And thinking what a chance this was for Minta and Paul and Lily to see her, and feeling what an amazing piece of luck it was that she herself had her, and that she would never grow up and never go away from home, she said, like a child, “We thought we’d go down to the beach and watch the waves.”
18.10: All at once, for no reason whatever, Mrs. Ramsay was like a girl of twenty, brimming with fun. A holiday mood seized her out of nowhere. Of course they must go; of course they must go, she cried, laughing; and running quickly down the last three or four stairs, she turned from one of them to the next, laughing, pulling Minta’s wrap around her, saying how she only wished she could come too — and would they be very late, and did any of them have a watch?
18.11: “Yes, Paul does,” Minta said. Out of a small chamois-leather case Paul slid a beautiful gold watch to show her. And holding it out on his palm in front of her, he felt, “She knows everything. I don’t need to say a word.” What he was saying to her, as he showed her the watch, was, “I’ve done it, Mrs. Ramsay. I owe it all to you.” And looking at the gold watch lying in his hand, Mrs. Ramsay felt: What extraordinary luck Minta has! She’s marrying a man who keeps his gold watch in a chamois-leather bag!
18.12: “Oh, how I wish I could come with you!” she cried. But something held her back, something so strong that it never even crossed her mind to ask what it was. Naturally, going with them was out of the question. Still, she would have liked to go, if it weren’t for the other thing; and amused by the absurdity of what she had been thinking (what luck to marry a man with a chamois-leather bag for his watch), she went, smiling, into the other room, where her husband was sitting reading.

19.0: Naturally, she told herself as she came in, she had had to come in here to fetch something she wanted. The first thing she wanted was to sit in one particular chair under one particular lamp. But she wanted something more besides, though what it was she did not know, could not think. Picking up her stocking and starting to knit, she glanced at her husband and saw that he did not want to be disturbed; that much was obvious. Whatever he was reading moved him deeply. He was half smiling, and then she could tell he was keeping his feelings under control. He was flipping the pages over. He was playing it out — maybe he fancied himself the man in the book. What book was it, she wondered. Oh, one of old Sir Walter Scott’s, she saw, tilting her lampshade so the light fell on her knitting. Because Charles Tansley had been saying (she looked up, half expecting to hear books crash to the floor overhead) — had been saying that nobody reads Scott any more. So her husband had thought, “That’s what they’ll say about me,” and had gone and fetched one of those books. And if he decided that Charles Tansley was right, he would accept it where Scott was concerned. (As he read she could see him weighing it up, considering, setting this against that.) But he would not accept it about himself. About himself he was always uneasy. That worried her. He would forever be fretting over his own books — will they be read, are they any good, why aren’t they better, what do people think of me? She didn’t like thinking of him that way; and wondering whether they had guessed at dinner why he turned so irritable all of a sudden when the talk was of fame and books that last, and whether the children were laughing about it, she gave the stocking a twitch; and around her lips and forehead all the fine lines appeared, as though cut with steel tools, and she grew still, like a tree that has been tossing and trembling and now, when the wind dies down, settles into quiet, one leaf after another.
19.1: None of it mattered, she thought. A great man, a great book, fame — who could say? She knew nothing about such things. But it was just his way, his honesty — at dinner, for example, she had caught herself thinking, quite by instinct, If only he would speak! She trusted him entirely. And letting all this go by, the way a diver slips past first a weed, then a straw, then a bubble, she felt again, sinking lower, what she had felt in the hall while the others talked: There is something I want — something I came here for. And, eyes shut, she sank further and further down, not quite knowing what it was. For a while she waited, knitting, wondering; and gradually the words they had said at dinner, “the China rose is all abloom and buzzing with the honey bee,” started washing to and fro across her mind in rhythm. And as they washed back and forth, words like small shaded lamps — a red one, a blue one, a yellow one — lit up in her mind’s darkness and seemed to leave their high perches and fly across and back again, or to call out and be answered by echoes. So she turned and felt around on the table next to her for a book.
19.2:
And all the lives we ever lived
And all the lives to be,
Are full of trees and changing leaves,
19.3: she murmured, pushing her needles into the stocking. Then she opened the book and started reading, dipping in here and there at random; and as she read, it felt to her like climbing backwards and upwards, shouldering her way up through petals that arched over her head, so that all she knew was that this one is white, or this one is red. To begin with, the words meant nothing to her at all.
19.4: Steer, hither steer your winged pines, all beaten Mariners
19.5: she read, and turned the page, and swung herself, zigzagging here and there, from line to line as if from branch to branch, from one red and white flower to the next, until she was roused by a small sound — her husband slapping his thighs. For a second their eyes met; but neither wanted to talk. There was nothing to say, and still something seemed to pass between them, from him to her. It was the life of the book, its power, its enormous humor, she knew, that made him slap his thighs. Don’t interrupt, he seemed to be telling her; don’t speak; just sit. And he read on. His lips twitched. It filled him up. It gave him strength. All the petty irritations and jabs of the evening went clean out of his head — how unbearably dull he found it to sit still while people went on eating and drinking forever, how snappish he had been with his wife, how thin-skinned, how he had minded when they skipped over his books as if they did not exist. But now, he felt, it didn’t matter a damn who got to Z (if thought ran like an alphabet from A to Z). Someone would get there — if not he, then another man. The strength and sanity of this writer, his feeling for plain and simple things, these fishermen, the poor crazed old creature in Mucklebackit’s cottage (all in Scott’s The Antiquary), made him feel so full of vigor, so freed of something, that he was stirred and triumphant and could not choke back his tears. Lifting the book slightly to hide his face, he let the tears fall, and shook his head from side to side, and lost himself entirely (apart from one or two thoughts about morality, and French novels versus English ones, and how Scott’s hands were tied, though his view was perhaps as true as the other one) — lost all his own worries and failures in poor Steenie’s drowning and Mucklebackit’s grief (that was Scott at his finest) and in the astonishing pleasure and energy it gave him.
19.6: Well, let them do better than that, he thought, finishing the chapter. He had the feeling of having argued with someone and won. Whatever they said, they could not do better than that; and his own standing felt more secure. The lovers were rubbish, he thought, gathering the whole thing together in his mind once more. That part’s rubbish, this part’s first-rate, he thought, setting one piece against another. But he would have to read it again. The overall shape of it escaped him. He must keep his verdict open. So he went back to his other thought — if the young men didn’t care for this, then of course they didn’t care for him either. You mustn’t complain, Mr. Ramsay told himself, trying to smother his wish to complain to his wife that the young men didn’t admire him. But he had made up his mind: he would not bother her again. At this point he looked over at her, reading. She looked very peaceful as she read. He liked to think that the others had all gone off and left the two of them alone. Going to bed with a woman was not the whole of life, he thought, turning back to Scott and Balzac, to the English novel and the French.
19.7: Mrs. Ramsay lifted her head, and, like someone lightly asleep, seemed to be saying that if he wanted her to wake she would — she really would; but if not, could she please go on sleeping, just a little longer, only a little longer? She was climbing up those branches, this way and that, putting her hand now on one flower, now on another.
19.8: Nor praise the deep vermilion in the rose,
19.9: she read; and reading, she felt she was rising higher, up to the top, up onto the peak. How satisfying it was! How restful! Every scrap and odd end of the day clung to this magnet; her mind felt swept out, clean. And then, suddenly, there it was, whole, taking shape in her hands, beautiful and reasonable, clear and complete — life’s essence drawn out of it and held here, rounded: the sonnet.
19.10: But she was growing aware that her husband was watching her. He was smiling at her, quizzical, as though teasing her gently for dozing in broad daylight; yet at the same time he was thinking, Keep reading. You don’t look sad now, he thought. He wondered what she was reading, and made her out to be more ignorant, more simple, than she was, because he liked to think of her as not clever, not bookish at all. Did she understand what she was reading, he wondered. Probably not. She was astonishingly beautiful. To him her beauty seemed, if such a thing could be, to be increasing.
19.11:
Yet seem’d it winter still, and, you away,
As with your shadow I with these did play,
19.13: “Well?” she said, looking up from her book and dreamily echoing his smile.
19.14: As with your shadow I with these did play,
19.15: she murmured, laying the book down on the table.
19.16: As she took up her knitting she wondered: what had happened since the last time she had seen him alone? She remembered getting dressed, and seeing the moon; Andrew holding his plate up too high at dinner; feeling low because of something William had said; the birds in the trees; the sofa on the landing; the children awake; Charles Tansley waking them with his books falling — oh no, she’d invented that; and Paul keeping his watch in a chamois-leather case. Which one should she tell him?
19.17: “They’re engaged,” she said as she began to knit. “Paul and Minta.”
19.18: “So I guessed,” he said. There was not much more to say about it. Her mind still went up and down, up and down, with the poetry; he still felt full of vigor, very plain-spoken, after reading about Steenie’s funeral. So they sat and said nothing. Then it dawned on her that she wanted him to speak.
19.19: Anything, anything, she thought, knitting on. Anything at all will do.
19.20: “How lovely it would be to marry a man who keeps his watch in a chamois-leather bag,” she said, because that was the kind of joke the two of them shared.
19.21: He snorted. He felt about this engagement what he always felt about every engagement: the girl is far too good for the young man. And slowly a question rose in her mind: why, then, do we want people to marry? What was the value, the meaning, of things? (Anything they said now would be true.) Please say something, she thought, longing only to hear his voice. Because the shadow, the thing that wrapped the two of them round, was starting, she felt, to close in on her again. Say anything, she begged him silently, looking at him as if for help.
19.22: He said nothing, but swung the compass on his watch-chain to and fro, thinking about Scott’s novels and Balzac’s. Yet through the dusky walls of their closeness — for they were drawing together without meaning to, coming side by side, very near — she could feel his mind like a hand lifted over hers, throwing it into shade. And now that her thoughts were turning in a direction he disliked, toward what he called her “pessimism,” he began to fidget, though he still did not speak — putting a hand to his forehead, twisting a strand of hair, letting it drop.
19.23: “You won’t get that stocking finished tonight,” he said, pointing at it. That was just what she wanted — the edge in his voice as he scolded her. If he says being pessimistic is wrong, then it’s probably wrong, she thought; the marriage will turn out fine.
19.24: “No,” she said, smoothing the stocking flat on her knee, “I won’t get it finished.”
19.25: And then what? She could feel that he was still looking at her, but that the look was different now. He wanted something — the thing she always found so hard to give him: he wanted her to say that she loved him. And that, no, she could not do. Talking came so much more easily to him than to her. He was able to say things — she never was. So of course it was always he who said them; and then, for some reason, he would suddenly resent it and reproach her. A heartless woman, he called her; she never once told him she loved him. But that wasn’t true — it wasn’t true. It was only that she never could put what she felt into words. Wasn’t there a crumb on his coat? Nothing she could do for him? She got up and stood at the window holding the reddish-brown stocking, partly to turn away from him and partly because now, with him watching, she did not mind looking at the Lighthouse. For she knew he had turned his head when she turned; he was watching her. She knew what he was thinking: You are more beautiful than ever. And she felt very beautiful. Won’t you tell me just this once that you love me? That was what he was thinking, because he was worked up — what with Minta, and his book, and the day coming to an end, and their quarrel about going to the Lighthouse. But she couldn’t; she couldn’t say it. Then, knowing he was watching her, instead of speaking she turned around, the stocking in her hands, and looked at him. And as she looked at him she began to smile, for although she had not said a word, he knew — of course he knew — that she loved him. He could not deny it. And smiling, she looked out of the window and said (thinking to herself, Nothing on earth can equal this happiness) —
19.26: “Yes, you were right. It’s going to be wet tomorrow.” She hadn’t said it, but he knew. And she looked at him, smiling. For once again she had triumphed.

20.0: “Well, only the future can tell us that,” Mr. Bankes said as he came in from the terrace.
20.1: “It’s nearly too dark to see anything,” said Andrew, coming up from the beach.
20.2: “One can scarcely tell which is sea and which is land,” said Prue.
20.3: “Are we leaving that light burning?” Lily asked as they took off their coats inside.
20.5: “Andrew,” she called over her shoulder, “just go and put out the hall light.”
20.6: One after another the lamps were all put out — except that Mr. Carmichael, who liked lying awake a while reading Virgil, kept his candle alight somewhat longer than everyone else.

21.0: So, with the lamps all put out, the moon gone down, and a thin rain drumming on the roof, a great downpour of darkness began. Nothing, it seemed, could survive the flood, the sheer abundance of darkness, which crept in at keyholes and cracks, stole around window blinds, came into bedrooms, and swallowed up here a jug and basin, there a bowl of red and yellow dahlias, there the sharp edges and solid bulk of a chest of drawers. It was not only the furniture that was blurred together; there was hardly anything left of body or mind by which you could say, “This is he,” or “This is she.” Sometimes a hand was raised as if to grasp something or fend something off, or somebody groaned, or somebody laughed aloud as if sharing a joke with nothingness.
21.1: Nothing stirred in the drawing-room or the dining-room or on the staircase. Only, through the rusty hinges and the swollen, sea-damp woodwork, certain breaths of air, broken off from the body of the wind (the house was ramshackle, after all), crept around corners and ventured indoors. You could almost imagine them, as they came into the drawing-room, questioning and wondering, playing with the loose flap of hanging wallpaper, asking: would it hang much longer, when would it fall? Then, smoothly brushing the walls, they passed on thoughtfully, as if asking the red and yellow roses on the wallpaper whether they would fade, and questioning (gently, for they had time to spare) the torn letters in the wastepaper basket, the flowers, the books, all of which were now open to them — asking, Were they allies? Were they enemies? How long would they last?
21.2: So, guided by some stray light from an uncovered star, or a wandering ship, or even the Lighthouse, with its pale footfall on stair and mat, the little breaths of air climbed the staircase and nosed around the bedroom doors. But here, surely, they must stop. Whatever else may perish and disappear, what lies here is steadfast. Here you might say to those sliding lights, those fumbling airs that breathe and bend over the bed itself: here you can neither touch nor destroy. At which, wearily, ghostlike, as if they had feather-light fingers and the light persistence of feathers, they would look once at the shut eyes and the loosely clasped fingers, and wearily fold their garments and disappear. And so, nosing, rubbing, they went to the window on the staircase, to the servants’ bedrooms, to the boxes in the attics; coming down again, they whitened the apples on the dining-room table, fumbled at the petals of the roses, tried the picture on the easel, brushed the mat and blew a little sand along the floor. At last, giving up, they all stopped together, gathered together, sighed together; all together they let out an aimless gust of lament, to which some door in the kitchen answered: it swung wide, let nothing in, and slammed shut.
21.3: [At this point Mr. Carmichael, who was reading Virgil, blew out his candle. It was after midnight.]

22.0: But what, after all, is one night? A short space of time, especially when the darkness fades so soon, and so soon a bird sings, a cock crows, or a faint green stirs, like a turning leaf, in the hollow of the wave. Night, however, follows night. Winter holds a whole pack of them in reserve and deals them out equally, evenly, with tireless fingers. They lengthen; they darken. Some of them hold up clear planets, plates of brightness. The autumn trees, ravaged as they are, take on the gleam of tattered flags glowing in the gloom of cool cathedral vaults, where gold letters on marble pages describe death in battle, and bones bleaching and burning far away in Indian sands. The autumn trees shine in the yellow moonlight, in the light of harvest moons — the light that softens the energy of labor, and smooths the stubble, and brings the wave lapping blue to the shore.
22.1: It seemed now as if, moved by human repentance and all its toil, divine goodness had drawn back the curtain and shown, behind it, single and distinct, the hare standing upright; the wave falling; the boat rocking — things which, if we deserved them, would be ours always. But alas, divine goodness twitches the cord and draws the curtain shut; it does not please him; he covers his treasures in a drenching of hail, and so breaks them, so scatters them, that it seems impossible their calm should ever return, or that we should ever put together a perfect whole from their fragments, or read the clear words of truth in the littered pieces. For our repentance earns only a glimpse; our toil, only a rest.
22.2: The nights now are full of wind and destruction. The trees plunge and bend, and their leaves fly helter-skelter until the lawn is plastered with them and they lie packed in gutters, choke the rain-pipes and litter the damp paths. The sea, too, tosses itself and breaks itself; and if some sleeper, imagining that he might find on the beach an answer to his doubts, someone to share his solitude, should throw off his bedclothes and go down alone to walk on the sand, no image that seems to serve him with divine readiness comes easily to hand, bringing the night to order and making the world reflect the range of the soul. The hand dwindles in his hand; the voice bellows in his ear. It would almost seem useless, in such confusion, to ask the night those questions — what, and why, and for what purpose — that tempt the sleeper from his bed to look for an answer.
22.3: [Stumbling along a passage one dark morning, Mr. Ramsay stretched out his arms; but, Mrs. Ramsay having died rather suddenly the night before, he stretched his arms out. They stayed empty.]

23.0: So, with the house empty and the doors locked and the mattresses rolled up, those stray breaths of air, the advance guard of great armies, blustered in, brushed the bare boards, nibbled and fanned, and met nothing in bedroom or drawing-room that fully resisted them — only hangings that flapped, wood that creaked, the bare legs of tables, saucepans and china already furred, tarnished, cracked. What people had shed and left behind — a pair of shoes, a shooting cap, some faded skirts and coats in the wardrobes — these alone kept the human shape, and in the emptiness showed how once they had been filled and brought to life; how once hands had been busy with hooks and buttons; how once the looking-glass had held a face, had held a hollowed-out world in which a figure turned, a hand flashed, the door opened, and in came children rushing and tumbling, and went out again. Now, day after day, the light turned its clear image on the opposite wall, like a flower reflected in water. Only the shadows of the trees, tossing in the wind, bowed low on the wall and for a moment darkened the pool in which the light reflected itself; or birds, flying past, made a soft spot flutter slowly across the bedroom floor.
23.1: So loveliness reigned, and stillness, and together they made the shape of loveliness itself, a form that life had left; solitary, like a pool at evening, far off, seen from a train window, vanishing so quickly that the pool, pale in the evening, is hardly robbed of its solitude, though it has once been seen. Loveliness and stillness clasped hands in the bedroom; and among the shrouded jugs and sheeted chairs, even the prying of the wind, and the soft noses of the clammy sea airs, rubbing, snuffling, repeating and repeating their questions — “Will you fade? Will you perish?” — hardly disturbed the peace, the indifference, the air of pure integrity, as if the question they asked scarcely needed an answer: we remain.
23.2: Nothing, it seemed, could break that image, spoil that innocence, or disturb the swaying cloak of silence which, week after week, in the empty room, wove into itself the falling cries of birds, ships hooting, the drone and hum of the fields, a dog’s bark, a man’s shout, and folded them around the house in silence. Only once did a board spring loose on the landing; once, in the middle of the night, with a roar, with a rupture, as when after centuries of stillness a rock tears itself from the mountain and hurtles crashing into the valley, one fold of the shawl came loose and swung back and forth. Then peace came down again; and the shadow wavered; the light bowed to its own image in adoration on the bedroom wall — when Mrs. McNab, tearing the veil of silence with hands that had stood in the washtub, grinding it under boots that had crunched the shingle, came as she had been told to open all the windows and dust the bedrooms.

24.0: As she lurched (for she rolled like a ship at sea) and leered (for her eyes never fell on anything directly, but only with a sidelong glance that begged off the scorn and anger of the world — she was witless, she knew it), as she clutched the banisters and hauled herself upstairs and rolled from room to room, she sang. Rubbing the glass of the long mirror and leering sideways at her swaying figure, she let a sound come from her lips — something that had perhaps been cheerful on the stage twenty years before, had been hummed and danced to, but now, coming from this toothless, bonneted caretaker, was robbed of meaning. It was like the voice of witlessness, of humor, of persistence itself, trodden down but springing up again; so that as she lurched along, dusting, wiping, she seemed to be saying how it was all one long sorrow and trouble, how it was getting up and going to bed again, and getting things out and putting them away again. It had not been easy or cozy, this world she had known for close on seventy years. She was bowed down with weariness. How long, she asked, creaking and groaning on her knees under the bed, dusting the boards, how long is it to go on? But she hobbled to her feet again, pulled herself up, and again, with her sidelong leer that slipped and turned aside even from her own face and her own sorrows, stood and gaped in the glass, smiling at nothing, and began again the old amble and hobble, taking up mats, putting down china, looking sideways in the glass — as if, after all, she had her consolations; as if some incorrigible hope really did twine itself around her dirge. There must have been visions of joy at the washtub, say, with her children (though two had been born out of wedlock and one had deserted her), or at the pub, drinking, or turning over odds and ends in her drawers. There must have been some break in the dark, some channel in the depths of obscurity through which enough light came to twist her face into a grin in the glass, and make her, turning to her work again, mumble out the old music-hall song. Meanwhile the mystics, the visionaries, walked the beach, stirred a puddle, looked at a stone, and asked themselves, “What am I?” “What is this?” — and suddenly an answer was granted them (what it was they could not say), so that they were warm in the frost and had comfort in the desert. But Mrs. McNab went on drinking and gossiping as before.
